extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, late-night talk show writers, and aspiring television writers (WGA members and entrants)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, production-focused guidance for writing and producing a nightly late-night talk show (monologues, sketches, recurring segments) including writers' room practices, hiring, and show voice development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue-volume strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Monologue writers collectively try to generate anywhere from 12 to 15 jokes for every show, producing a large volume of material so the best 10–15 make it on air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "They, as a group collectively, write anywhere from 200 to 300 jokes in order to yield the 10 to 15 that we do on air." Emphasizes a 'volume game': write immediately as news breaks, generate many options, then narrow down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch lead time and daily sketch meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch writers work with longer lead times (e.g., a Thursday sketch can begin Monday/Tuesday) and participate in a daily sketch meeting to receive notes and do rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "They come into my office where I have a sketch meeting every day. That’s at 11 o’clock in the morning... we start looking at it on Monday so we have time to give notes and then they can turn in rewrites." Plan sketches earlier than day-of; allow iterative notes and rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Closer Look segment workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Closer Look" segments have a nightly first draft produced before the writers' room and then are collectively edited into shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We have a writer named Sal Gentile who is putting together first drafts of that every night before we come in. Then, we collectively start adding jokes and making cuts and putting it into a shape that gets it ready to go for our show." Combine a fast first draft with group editing for shape and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host comfort defines performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Host comfort (e.g., sitting behind a desk vs. standing) strongly affects delivery and the show's tone; choose formats that maximize host comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "These shows are so much about host comfort... I was a lot more comfortable starting behind a desk than I’d ever been standing and doing a monologue." Format choices should prioritize what makes the host perform best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and staging influence voice (graphics/keys)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing staging (curtain vs. desk with graphics/keys) shifts the show’s feel from conversational to newsier, which should align with the host’s background and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We got to change the backdrop of the show... a little bit more jokes with graphics and keys. That naturally moved it from a less conversational place to a more newsy place." Use visual/production elements to support the show's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire people who make you laugh (trust your taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: When hiring writers, prioritize making-you-laugh over pedigree—trust the host/showrunner’s taste as a primary hiring filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lorne’s advice: 'if somebody makes you laugh, no matter how green they are... if they make you laugh, you probably won’t go wrong hiring them.' Taste is a late-night host's defining asset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate effort to build writer diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: To have a range of authentic voices (especially for topics like race/equality), you must make an extra effort when assembling the writing staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "When you want to have a show that has a lot of different voices, you have to make the extra effort when you’re putting together your writing staff." Diversity also enables sketches the host can't perform personally (e.g., 'Jokes Seth Can’t Tell').

rubrics_metrics.name: Value writer-performers and on-air writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiring writers who can perform increases the show’s capabilities and allows the staff to be integrated on-air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing writing staff on-air 'increases the ability of what you can do.' A deep bench of performers-writers expands sketch possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find sketches with a strong take
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches should have a clear, strong point of view or 'take' that makes them feel purposeful and translatable from page to stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Boston Accent... It had a really strong take.' Strong takes make sketches that can 'easily could’ve been on SNL.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Play to your show's strengths; avoid mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure out what your show does best (often takes 18 months–2 years) and focus on delivering that instead of imitating other shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We try not to get caught doing something that we feel other shows do significantly better than us... it takes you 18 months to 2 years to figure out what those strengths are." Patience and self-knowledge guide creative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-night audience relationship and bombing recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Because late-night is nightly, you build audience rapport faster and can recover publicly from jokes that bomb by commenting or explaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If you have a joke that bombs, it’s not as bad an outcome as it would be at SNL, because you can comment on it... You can explain to the audience what your thought process was." Use the format's immediacy as an advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent rewriting and host editorial role
rubrics_metrics.description: The host often spends substantial time rewriting writers' drafts to inflect personal voice; the longer writers stay, the better they capture that voice, reducing host rewrite burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I do a lot of rewriting... I can spend the first two or three hours... adding jokes, taking out things that I don’t love and putting in a little bit more of my voice." Expect iterative editing and voice alignment over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily hustle and consistent output
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing a nightly show is intensive, requiring steady, daily labor and consistent output—'hustle and hustle and hustle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "When you work at a late-night show, you’re putting it on every day. It’s basically like you’re a dock worker working at the shipyard." Plan for continual deadlines and production cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source writers from varied backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit writers from a wide range of backgrounds (social media, satirical outlets, improv) to broaden the pool of voices and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We hired people from all different walks of life: people that we found on Twitter, people who worked at THE ONION and improvisers from Chicago." Nontraditional hiring channels can yield strong talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of political content and audience appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously monitor whether the audience's appetite for political material has changed; let the news guide topical coverage rather than forcing politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We are constantly trying to get a sense if the audience has changed at all, if there’s a different appetite for the amount of politics we do... As far as how we approach the news every day, we don’t decide what’s in the news. The news does that for us." Balance topicality with audience tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited transformative interviews with politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians are typically 'programmed' and unlikely to have a revelatory moment on a talk show; plan interviews with realistic expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Pretty much all politicians... you are never going to say something to somebody like Hillary Clinton or Ted Cruz and watch their eyes like, 'Wow.' It’s too late for all of them." Consider whether a political guest will produce meaningful television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network context and lead-in impact
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong lead-in (e.g., THE TONIGHT SHOW) and network support can give a late-night show freedom to pursue its chosen tone and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We’re lucky to be on after THE TONIGHT SHOW... It’s nice that we can do the show we want and that the network hasn’t been opposed." Consider scheduling and executive buy-in when shaping show identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow time to find your show's voice (patience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that it takes significant time—roughly 18 months—to figure out a show’s identity and what works; patience is part of the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "When I started the show, he said, 'Look, it takes 18 months to figure it out.' ... Sure enough, it was about 18 months to the day that I finally thought, 'I got to sit behind the desk.'" Plan for a developmental period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain collaborative shorthand for side projects
rubrics_metrics.description: When doing additional projects (e.g., Documentary Now!), a shorthand among collaborators lets you produce quality work in limited windows without lengthy retreats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "DOC NOW was such a passion project... We could reach out and communicate via email and figure out who was going to write what." Use established working relationships to manage parallel projects during hiatuses.
